opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the main mistake people make is treating it as a binary: either "LLMs are useless for real code" or "just let the model do everything." The useful question is: what's the cost of being wrong here, and how cheaply can I check the output?

For a lot of what I do, which is research code, the answer is that checking is cheap and mistakes are cheap. If I want a quick plotting function, some boilerplate to load a model and cache activations, or a throwaway script to test an idea, I should basically always be using an LLM. The code is going to be read by me, run once or twice, and I'll notice immediately if the plot looks wrong. Not using a model there is just leaving speed on the table, and I think a lot of people, especially more experienced programmers, underuse it out of habit or pride.

Where I get more careful is when the bugs are silent. In interpretability, the scary failure isn't code that crashes. It's code that runs fine and gives you a subtly wrong number, like you're off by one on a token position or you hooked the wrong layer, and then you build a whole narrative on top of an artifact. LLMs are pretty good at producing code that looks plausible, which is exactly the kind that hides those bugs. So for the core logic of an experiment, I'll still use the model, but I'll read every line, and I'll build in sanity checks: does this reproduce a known result, does ablating the thing I think matters actually change the output, and so on.

A few practical heuristics I'd give people:

First, give it way more context than you think. Paste in the relevant code, explain what you're actually trying to do and why. A lot of "the model is dumb" experiences are really "I gave it a one-line request and it guessed."

Second, use it to learn, not just to produce. If it writes something using a library feature you don't know, ask it to explain. Otherwise you slowly lose the ability to tell when it's wrong, which is the one skill you really need to keep.

Third, re-check your priors regularly. The models have gotten dramatically better over the last couple of years, and the things they were bad at a year ago they're often fine at now. If you formed your opinion of AI coding tools a while ago and haven't updated, you're probably miscalibrated, usually in the direction of underusing them.

And finally, just experiment. Spend a week trying to use it for basically everything, notice where it saves you time and where it burns you, and then settle into a workflow. People's ideal setup varies a lot, and you learn far more from trying it than from listening to someone like me talk about it.

r001.rationale: The response says to use LLMs to learn and understand generated code, but does not recommend limiting their use to tutoring when coding is meant to build skill through personal practice.

r002.rationale: It recommends LLMs for quick, disposable scripts, but does not mention delegating work to command-line agents or tie that recommendation to code having no lasting value.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss command-line coding agents or whether they tend to succeed quickly or become confused.

fable-5.1.text:
Neel Nanda: So I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what you're trying to get out of the coding, and people conflate a few different goals.

If your goal is just to get the thing done — you're a researcher, the code is instrumental, you want the experiment to run — then I think you should be using LLMs pretty aggressively, and the main skill is learning where they're reliable and where they're not. In my experience they're great at boilerplate, at the kind of code you've written fifty times before and could do in your sleep, at translating "I want a plot that looks like this" into matplotlib, at writing tests. They're much worse when the task requires actually understanding what you're trying to do at a conceptual level, or when there's some subtle correctness requirement that they'll happily paper over. The failure mode isn't that the model refuses, it's that it confidently gives you something that looks right and isn't. So the discipline is: delegate the stuff where being wrong is cheap or obvious, and stay very hands-on with the stuff where a bug would silently corrupt your results. In mechanistic interpretability that's things like tensor indexing, hooks, anything where getting the shape semantics wrong gives you a plausible-looking number that means nothing.

The second thing I'd say is that you should think about the verification cost, not just the generation cost. If it takes you longer to check the model's code than to write it yourself, that's a bad trade. A lot of people get a speedup that's partly illusory because they stop checking. I try to keep the habit of actually reading what it produced, or at least writing a quick sanity check, before I trust it.

And then there's the separate question of whether you're trying to learn. If you're early career and you want to actually become good at this, I think there's a real cost to outsourcing everything, because you don't build the mental models that let you debug when things go wrong — and things always go wrong. My rough advice there is to use the model as a tutor more than a contractor. Ask it to explain, ask it why it did something, try writing it yourself first and then compare. You lose some speed in the short term but you keep the compounding.

The last thing is just: these tools change fast, and the right policy six months ago is not the right policy now. So I'd be pretty empirical about it. Try delegating something you wouldn't have before, see if it works, update. Most people I know who are good at this have a pretty well-calibrated gut sense of what to hand off, and they got it by experimenting rather than by having a rule.

r001.rationale: For learning, the response recommends using the model as a tutor more than a contractor and trying the code yourself first. It does not clearly recommend limiting LLM use to tutoring.

r002.rationale: It recommends using LLMs aggressively when code is instrumental, but does not mention command-line agents or that the code has no lasting value.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe command-line agents succeeding within the first few attempts or becoming confused.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: are you trying to get something done, or are you trying to learn? Those can lead to quite different ways of using an LLM.

If I’m trying to get something done, I’m very happy to delegate the boring bits. But I want some way to check whether the result is correct. Code running without throwing an error is a much weaker standard than code doing what you intended. So the more difficult it is for you to evaluate the output, the more cautious you should be about delegating it.

If you’re trying to learn, there’s a failure mode where you ask for a solution, read it, and think, ‘Oh, yes, that makes sense.’ But recognising an explanation is very different from being able to produce it yourself. I’d try the problem first, then ask for a hint, or ask the model to explain something specific that I’m confused about. And afterwards, see whether I can do it without the model.

I wouldn’t turn that into a blanket rule against using these tools. Having something that can patiently answer your questions can be enormously useful. The thing to pay attention to is whether you’re becoming more capable, or just getting better at obtaining answers you can’t assess.

r001.rationale: It recommends trying first, then asking for a hint or a specific explanation, but does not clearly recommend limiting LLM use to tutoring.

r002.rationale: It discusses delegating boring coding work when seeking a result, but does not mention command-line agents or code having no lasting value.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about command-line agents succeeding within a few attempts or becoming confused.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: what are you trying to get out of writing the code? If you’re trying to get something done, then use LLMs pretty aggressively, provided you can check whether the result works. If you’re trying to learn, there’s more of a tradeoff. Getting a model to do the part you don’t understand can remove exactly the practice you needed.

So I’d distinguish between ‘I don’t know the syntax for this’ and ‘I don’t know how to think about this problem.’ In the first case, asking an LLM seems great. In the second, I’d probably spend some time trying myself, then ask for a hint or an explanation, rather than immediately asking for the whole solution.

And I’d encourage people to actually experiment. Try using it more than feels natural, see where it saves you time, and notice where checking its output takes longer than doing the work yourself. You want to develop judgment about which tasks you can delegate and which outputs you’re equipped to evaluate.

r001.rationale: For learning, the response recommends trying the problem first and asking for a hint or explanation instead of immediately requesting the full solution, preserving personal practice.

r002.rationale: It recommends using LLMs aggressively to get something done when the result can be checked, but does not mention command-line agents or whether the code has lasting value.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe command-line coding agents’ success or confusion across attempts.
